title: Vision Token Compression with Linear Attention
open: Can V-CoLA's token compression be extended to vision-language architectures built purely on linear attention, without periodic softmax-attention layers? Answering this formally means understanding how the uniqueness-aware importance criterion behaves when the grounding Gated DeltaNet-style interactions that shaped its design are absent.
solved_when: A formulation of V-CoLA's uniqueness-aware importance criterion is given for linear-attention (softmax-free) vision backbones, with analysis showing when it remains valid for token compression in such architectures.
why: The method is currently grounded in the Gated DeltaNet formulation that underlies several recent hybrid VLMs; a principled extension would make the compression applicable to purely linear-attention vision encoders rather than only hybrids.

title: Leaner Transformers Can Easily Learn to Cluster
open: Are the extra dimensions used in the model — beyond those strictly needed for representing the data — actually necessary for a transformer to learn a clustering algorithm competitive with Lloyd's algorithm? Put formally, it is unclear whether one can remove the additional dimensions (denoted with the dimensional slack parameters in the paper) while still matching Lloyd's algorithm's clustering quality.
solved_when: A proof or construction showing that a (leaner) transformer without the additional dimensions can learn a clustering algorithm competitive with Lloyd's algorithm — or, conversely, a lower bound showing those extra dimensions are provably necessary for such competitiveness.
why: It separates true representational requirements from artifacts of the construction, determining how lean a transformer must be to implement Lloyd-style clustering and clarifying the role of dimensional overhead in learned algorithms.

title: Computations of the slice genus and the unknotting number of links via
open: Among the 249 prime knots with up to ten crossings, the unknotting number remains undetermined for ten of them. Can these ten values be computed, or can a practical algorithm be developed that determines the unknotting number for every knot in this range?
solved_when: The unknotting number is known for all 249 prime knots with up to ten crossings, including the ten currently unresolved cases.
why: It would complete the classical knot tables in the smallest crossing range, providing exact data that constrains sliceness, genus bounds, and deformation classes for these knots.

title: Computations of the slice genus and the unknotting number of links via
open: Is every slice knot ribbon? Since every ribbon surface is in particular a slice surface, the minimum defining the slice genus is taken over a larger set of surfaces, giving an inequality between the corresponding genera; whether this inequality can be strict for slice knots is the content of a long-standing open problem raised by Fox in 1961.
status: The problem is stated as open in the source (2026), arXiv paper 2610.10206, where it is traced back to Fox's 1961 question; no resolution is recorded there.
solved_when: A proof that every slice knot is ribbon, or a counterexample exhibiting a slice knot that is not ribbon (equivalently, a case where the slice-genus inequality over the larger set of slice surfaces is strict).
why: It would determine whether the class of slice knots genuinely extends beyond ribbon knots, sharpening which surfaces can realize the slice genus and constraining computations of the slice genus and related link invariants.

title: Edge Accuracy Is Not Enough: Why Dynamics-Learned Structure Fails to T — conjecture conj:dominance
open: When a graph structure $G$ is learned from an objective misaligned with the inverse task, must the approximation error dominate the estimation error regardless of sample size or threshold selection, whenever the forward and inverse tasks have fundamentally different optimal structures $G^*_{\text{dyn}} \neq G^*_{\text{loc}}$? A formal answer would establish a dominance principle: no amount of data or tuning can close the gap once the learned structure optimizes the wrong objective.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given of the dominance conjecture: for dynamics-learned $G$ under objective misalignment, approximation error exceeds estimation error for all sample sizes and all threshold choices whenever $G^*_{\text{dyn}} \neq G^*_{\text{loc}}$.
why: It explains why high edge accuracy in learned graphs still yields poor inverse-task performance, and would tell practitioners when more data or better thresholding cannot help and the learning objective itself must change.

title: Global Correspondence-Free Point Set Alignment through Assignme
open: Can optimal partial matchings between point sets under translation be found by a polynomial-time enumeration procedure? In other words, is there a polynomial algorithm that enumerates all optimal partial matchings for point set alignment under translation, without needing precomputed correspondences?
status: Stated as open in the source (2026), the paper arXiv:2610.10408; no partial results are recorded.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is given that enumerates optimal partial matchings under translation, with a proof of correctness and polynomial complexity.
why: It would settle whether globally optimal correspondence-free point set alignment is computationally tractable, removing the need for heuristics or correspondence assumptions in registration problems.
